seo.shortDescription: Searchable duty table for all 217 HTS Chapter 38 lines — pesticides and disinfectants, activated carbon, fatty acids, biodiesel, silicon wafers, diagnostic reagents, refrigerant blends and other chemical preparations — with the 2026 Section 301, Canada Section 338 and China duties and the AD/CVD orders.

overview.intro:
Chapter 38 is the chemical catch-all: artificial graphite, activated carbon, tall oil, turpentine and rosin, pesticides, herbicides and disinfectants (3808), finishing agents, fluxes, fuel and lubricant additives, rubber chemicals, catalysts, doped silicon wafers (3818), brake fluid and antifreeze, diagnostic reagents (3822), industrial fatty acids and alcohols (3823), the 3824 preparations n.e.s., chemical waste, biodiesel (3826) and refrigerant blends (3827). Base rates run from Free to 6.5%, and the U.S. imported **$22.15B** of these goods in 2025.

The extra duties matter more than the base rates. Since July 24, 2026 the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** add 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies, including Japan, Korea, the EU, the UK, India and Mexico, with only doped wafers exempt for everyone; Chinese goods pay the 2018–2019 Section 301 duties plus 12.5% (wafers 50%), and since August 22, 2026 **Canadian fatty acids, sorbitol and some other preparations pay 50%** under Section 338, even with a USMCA claim. Several products — biodiesel from Argentina and Indonesia, activated carbon, HFC blends and pool chlorine from China, 2,4-D, and (preliminarily) fatty acids from Indonesia and Malaysia — also carry **antidumping or countervailing duties**, which the tariff calculator does not include.

productGroups.label: Artificial graphite & carbon pastes
productGroups.blurb: Artificial graphite, colloidal graphite, carbonaceous electrode pastes and other carbon preparations: 7 lines, Free to 4.9%. Includes spherical graphite (3801.10.50.10) and silicon-containing active anode material for batteries (3801.90.00.10, split out February 1, 2026).

productGroups.label: Activated carbon
productGroups.blurb: Activated carbon from coal, coconut or other sources, bone black and activated clays: 6 lines, 2.5% to 5.8%.

productGroups.label: Tall oil
productGroups.blurb: Crude or refined tall oil from kraft pulping: 1 line, Free.

productGroups.label: Lignin sulfonates & wood-pulp lyes
productGroups.blurb: Residual lyes from wood-pulp manufacture: lignin sulfonic acid and its salts are Free, other lyes 3.7%. Tall oil is 3803.

productGroups.label: Turpentine & pine oil
productGroups.blurb: Gum, wood or sulfate turpentine (5%), pine oil (Free) and other terpenic oils (3.7%): 3 lines.

productGroups.label: Rosin & ester gums
productGroups.blurb: Gum rosin and other rosin and resin acids (5%), rosin salts (3.7%), ester gums (6.5%) and other rosin derivatives (4.2%): 5 lines.

productGroups.label: Wood tar & brewers' pitch
productGroups.blurb: Wood tar, wood tar oils, wood creosote, wood naphtha, vegetable pitch and brewers' pitch: 1 line, 0.1%.

productGroups.label: Pesticides, herbicides & disinfectants
productGroups.blurb: Insecticides, fungicides, herbicides (glyphosate, glufosinate), plant-growth regulators, rodenticides, disinfectants and alcohol hand sanitizer (3808.94.50.80): 38 lines, Free to 6.5%. Pesticides also need EPA registration and a Notice of Arrival before the shipment lands.

productGroups.label: Textile, paper & leather finishing agents
productGroups.blurb: Finishing agents, dye carriers and mordants for the textile, paper and leather industries: 6 lines, 6% to 6.5% (starch-based: 2.2¢/kg + 3%).

productGroups.label: Pickling preparations & soldering fluxes
productGroups.blurb: Metal pickling preparations, soldering and welding powders and pastes, and fluxes: 4 lines, Free to 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Fuel & lubricant additives
productGroups.blurb: Antiknock preparations, oxidation inhibitors, viscosity improvers, anti-corrosives and other additives for fuel and lubricating oils: 6 lines, Free to 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Rubber accelerators, plasticizers & stabilizers
productGroups.blurb: Prepared rubber accelerators, compound plasticizers and antioxidant or stabilizer preparations for rubber or plastics (e.g. TMQ): 10 lines, Free to 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Fire-extinguisher charges
productGroups.blurb: Preparations and charges for fire extinguishers and charged extinguishing grenades: 2 lines, Free (wholly inorganic) or 3.7%.

productGroups.label: Solvents, thinners & paint removers
productGroups.blurb: Composite organic solvents and thinners, paint and varnish removers: 4 lines, 6% to 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Catalysts
productGroups.blurb: Supported catalysts with nickel, precious metals (platinum-group split out February 1, 2026) or other active substances, and other catalytic preparations: 8 lines, Free to 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Refractory cements & mortars
productGroups.blurb: Refractory cements, mortars, castables and dolomite ramming mix: 3 lines, Free or 3%.

productGroups.label: Mixed alkylbenzenes (LAB)
productGroups.blurb: Mixed linear alkylbenzenes (LAB) and other alkylbenzenes and alkylnaphthalenes: 3 lines, all 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Doped silicon wafers & electronic chemicals
productGroups.blurb: Doped silicon, silicon carbide and gallium arsenide wafers and other doped elements and compounds for electronics: 7 lines, all Free. Chinese wafers pay 50% under Section 301; wafers are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on other countries.

productGroups.label: Brake & hydraulic fluids
productGroups.blurb: Hydraulic brake fluids and other hydraulic transmission liquids with less than 70% petroleum oil: 2 lines, 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Antifreeze & deicing fluids
productGroups.blurb: Antifreezing preparations and prepared deicing fluids (engine coolant, aircraft deicer): 1 line, 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Culture media
productGroups.blurb: Prepared culture media for micro-organisms, including viral transport media: 2 lines, 5%.

productGroups.label: Diagnostic & laboratory reagents
productGroups.blurb: Diagnostic and laboratory reagents on a backing or prepared (test kits, reagent strips) and certified reference materials: 8 lines, all Free.

productGroups.label: Industrial fatty acids & fatty alcohols
productGroups.blurb: Stearic and oleic acid (2.1¢/kg plus 3.8% or 3.2%), tall oil fatty acids, palm and coconut fatty acids and fatty acid distillates, acid oils, and industrial fatty alcohols: 9 lines. Several are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty for the EU, Malaysia, Indonesia and others, and pay 50% from Canada under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Other chemical preparations (n.e.s.)
productGroups.blurb: The catch-all heading: foundry binders, concrete admixtures, sorbitol, mixtures containing listed persistent pollutants, cultured crystals, cathode-material mixtures, fatty acid ester mixtures and other chemical preparations: 48 lines, Free to 6.5%.

productGroups.label: Chemical, municipal & clinical waste
productGroups.blurb: Municipal waste, sewage sludge, clinical waste, waste solvents and other chemical-industry waste: 9 lines, all Free.

productGroups.label: Biodiesel
productGroups.blurb: Biodiesel (B100) at 4.6% and blends with less than 70% petroleum oil at 6.5%: 2 lines. Imported biodiesel does not earn the U.S. clean fuel production credit, and must meet EPA fuel and Renewable Fuel Standard rules.

productGroups.label: Refrigerant & other halogenated blends
productGroups.blurb: Mixtures of halogenated methane, ethane or propane derivatives — HFC refrigerant blends such as R-410A, R-404A and R-407C, HCFC and CFC blends, halons: 20 lines, 3.7% or 6.5%. Bulk HFC imports need EPA allowances.

workedExamples.title: Stearic acid from Canada
workedExamples.body: Stearic acid is on the Canada Section 338 list (note 51(b)(3)), so it pays **+50%** (9903.03.14) even when USMCA is claimed: with a USMCA claim the base rate is Free and the 10% Section 301 duty is lifted (9903.05.93), leaving **50%** — $50,000 on a $100,000 shipment. Without USMCA it is 2.1¢/kg + 3.8% + 10% + 50% (**2.1¢/kg + 63.8%**). The same stearic acid from Germany or Malaysia pays only its base rate (note 52(j)).

workedExamples.title: Glyphosate herbicide from China vs. India
workedExamples.body: Base rate 5%. From China it adds 25% (List 3, 9903.88.03) and 12.5% (2026 Section 301, 9903.05.31): **42.5%**, or $42,500 on $100,000. From India it is 5% + 10% (9903.05.44) = **15%**. A 2,4-D formulation (3808.93.15) from either country would also pay antidumping and countervailing duties, which the calculator does not include.

workedExamples.title: Biodiesel (B100) from Argentina
workedExamples.body: The tariff is 4.6% + 10% Section 301 (9903.05.22) = **14.6%**. On top come the 2018 antidumping and countervailing duty orders: an exporter without its own rate posts **74.63% + 71.87%** cash deposits. Imported biodiesel also does not earn the U.S. clean fuel production credit (section 45Z), which is limited to domestically produced fuel.

**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) separate chemically defined elements or compounds, except (1) artificial graphite (heading 3801); (2) insecticides, rodenticides, fungicides, herbicides, anti-sprouting products and plant-growth regulators, disinfectants and similar products put up as described in heading 3808; (3) products put up as charges for fire-extinguishers or in fire-extinguishing grenades (heading 3813); (4) certified reference materials specified in note 2; (5) products specified in note 3(a) or 3(c); (b) mixtures of chemicals with foodstuffs or other substances with nutritive value, of a kind used in the preparation of human foodstuffs (generally heading 2106); (c) products of heading 2404; (d) slag, ash and residues containing metals, arsenic or their mixtures and meeting note 3(a) or 3(b) to chapter 26 (heading 2620); (e) medicaments (heading 3003 or 3004); or (f) spent catalysts of a kind used for extracting base metals or making their compounds (heading 2620) or for recovering precious metal (heading 7112), and catalysts consisting of metals or metal alloys in the form of, for example, finely divided powder or woven gauze (section XIV or XV).

**Note 2.** (a) For heading 3822, "certified reference materials" are reference materials accompanied by a certificate stating the values of the certified properties, the methods used to determine them and the degree of certainty of each value, and suitable for analytical, calibrating or referencing purposes. (b) Except for products of chapter 28 or 29, heading 3822 takes precedence over any other heading for certified reference materials.

**Note 3.** Heading 3824 includes, and no other heading covers: (a) cultured crystals (other than optical elements) weighing not less than 2.5 g each, of magnesium oxide or of the halides of the alkali or alkaline-earth metals; (b) fusel oil and Dippel's oil; (c) ink removers put up for retail sale; (d) stencil correctors, other correcting fluids and correction tapes (other than those of heading 9612), put up for retail sale; and (e) fusible ceramic firing testers (for example, Seger cones).

**Note 4.** "Municipal waste" means waste collected from households, hotels, restaurants, hospitals, shops, offices and the like, road and pavement sweepings, and construction and demolition waste. It does not cover (a) materials or articles segregated from the waste (plastics, rubber, wood, paper, textiles, glass, metals, electrical and electronic waste and scrap, including spent batteries), which go in their own headings; (b) industrial waste; (c) waste pharmaceuticals (note 4(k) to chapter 30); or (d) clinical waste (note 6(a)).

**Note 5.** For heading 3825, "sewage sludge" is sludge from urban effluent treatment plants, including pre-treatment waste, scourings and unstabilized sludge. Stabilized sludge suitable for use as fertilizer is excluded (chapter 31).

**Note 6.** For heading 3825, "other wastes" means (a) clinical waste — contaminated waste from medical research, diagnosis, treatment or other medical, surgical, dental or veterinary procedures; (b) waste organic solvents; (c) wastes of metal pickling liquors, hydraulic fluids, brake fluids and anti-freezing fluids; and (d) other wastes from the chemical or allied industries. It does not cover wastes containing mainly petroleum oils or oils obtained from bituminous materials (heading 2710).

**Note 7.** For heading 3826, "biodiesel" means mono-alkyl esters of fatty acids of a kind used as a fuel, derived from animal, vegetable or microbial fats and oils, whether or not used.

**Subheading note 1.** Subheadings 3808.52 and 3808.59 cover only goods of heading 3808 containing one or more of: alachlor; aldicarb; aldrin; azinphos-methyl; binapacryl; camphechlor (toxaphene); captafol; carbofuran; chlordane; chlordimeform; chlorobenzilate; DDT; dieldrin; DNOC or its salts; dinoseb, its salts or esters; endosulfan; ethylene dibromide; ethylene dichloride; fluoroacetamide; heptachlor; hexachlorobenzene; HCH, including lindane; mercury compounds; methamidophos; monocrotophos; oxirane (ethylene oxide); parathion; parathion-methyl; pentachlorophenol, its salts or esters; perfluorooctane sulphonic acid and its salts; perfluorooctane sulphonamides; perfluorooctane sulphonyl fluoride; phosphamidon; 2,4,5-T, its salts or esters; tributyltin compounds; trichlorfon. (2026 Revision 21 deleted, as an erratum, a sentence that also placed dustable powder formulations of benomyl, carbofuran and thiram in 3808.59.)

**Subheading note 2.** Subheadings 3808.61 to 3808.69 cover only goods of heading 3808 containing alpha-cypermethrin, bendiocarb, bifenthrin, chlorfenapyr, cyfluthrin, deltamethrin, etofenprox, fenitrothion, lambda-cyhalothrin, malathion, pirimiphos-methyl or propoxur.

**Subheading note 3.** Subheadings 3824.81 to 3824.89 cover only mixtures and preparations containing one or more of: oxirane (ethylene oxide); PBBs; PCBs; PCTs; tris(2,3-dibromopropyl) phosphate; aldrin; camphechlor (toxaphene); chlordane; chlordecone; DDT; dieldrin; endosulfan; endrin; heptachlor; mirex; HCH, including lindane; pentachlorobenzene; hexachlorobenzene; perfluorooctane sulphonic acid and its salts; perfluorooctane sulphonamides; perfluorooctane sulphonyl fluoride; tetra-, penta-, hexa-, hepta- or octabromodiphenyl ethers; short-chain chlorinated paraffins (C10–C13, more than 48% chlorine by weight).

**Subheading note 4.** For subheadings 3825.41 and 3825.49, "waste organic solvents" are wastes containing mainly organic solvents, not fit for further use as presented as primary products, whether or not intended for recovery of the solvents.

**Statistical notes.** (1) Hand sanitizer reported under 3808.94.5080 must meet U.S. Food and Drug Administration requirements for disinfecting hand sanitizers. (2) 3818.00.0040 covers doped monocrystalline silicon wafers, round (circular), of a kind used for semiconductor fabrication, typically made to SEMI M1 standards. (3) 3818.00.0045 covers doped monocrystalline silicon wafers, pseudo-square or rectangular, of a kind used in solar photovoltaic cells. (4) For heading 3824, "biodiesel" means fatty acid esters of a kind used as fuel, derived from animal or vegetable fats and oils, whether or not used.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 38: Miscellaneous Chemical Products — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Chemical Tariff Updates 2026 — HTS Chapter 38: Section 301, Canada 338, China, Biodiesel | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 38 chemical imports since January 2025: the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and their exemptions, Canada's 50% Section 338 duty on fatty acids, China's 25%–50% Section 301 rates, and AD/CVD orders, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). None of the 209 Chapter 38 lines present in both editions changed its base rate; eight statistical lines are new — silicon-containing active anode material and platinum-group catalysts (February 1, 2026) and four kinds of doped silicon wafers (July 1, 2026). Revision 21 itself only corrected subheading note 1 of the chapter (a pesticide-classification sentence was deleted as an erratum).

The extra duties changed far more. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Canada, Mexico, China and the reciprocal tariff) **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** add 10% or 12.5% on goods of 60 economies, and almost all of Chapter 38 is covered: only doped wafers (3818) are on the general exemption list. Since **August 22, 2026** Canadian fatty acids, fatty alcohols, sorbitol, some lubricant additives and other preparations pay a **50% Section 338** duty even under USMCA. Chinese goods pay the 2018–2019 Section 301 duties (mostly 25%) plus 12.5%, and Chinese wafers 50%.

Separately, **antidumping and countervailing duties** apply to several Chapter 38 products (see the change log). They are set company by company by the Commerce Department, are listed below for reference, and are **not included in the tariff calculator**.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 38 from any country (the 2026 Section 301 action on 60 economies and the Brazil action; China's Section 301 lists; Canada's Section 338 duty; the Russia rates and Russian-aluminum Section 232 duty; the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties), plus the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on Chapter 38 products, which the tariff calculator does not model. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

The 25% and 7.5% List 2, 3 and 4A duties on Chinese Chapter 38 goods continue.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), with no Chapter 38 exemption. The rate is 0% in 2026; Nicaragua's 12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.58) applies now.

changes.title: Large-diameter graphite electrodes from China and India: preliminary dumping margins
changes.detail: Commerce preliminarily set antidumping cash deposits of 95.61% for China (China-wide) and 9.88% (Graphite India), 1.15% (HEG) and 3.53% (all others) for India, on top of the July 30, 2026 preliminary countervailing duties (China 103.49%, India 5.87% all others). The scope lists 3801.10.50.90 and 3801.90.00.50 as well as the electrode lines of Chapter 85.

changes.title: Fatty acids from Indonesia and Malaysia: preliminary dumping margins
changes.detail: Commerce preliminarily found dumping of certain fatty acids (stearic, oleic and other fatty acids of 3823.11, 3823.12, 3823.19.20 and 3823.19.40, which may also enter under 3824.99.41.90). Cash deposits: Indonesia 22.96% (Musim Mas), 12.31% (Wilmar Nabati), 19.49% (all others), with critical circumstances found for all others; Malaysia 4.46% (Evyap), 7.06% (Palm-Oleo), 5.22% (all others). They come on top of the July 23 preliminary countervailing duties. Final determinations are due in early 2027.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 list revised; Chapter 38 lines unchanged
changes.detail: Proclamation 11065 changed the products on the Section 338 list (9903.03.14) and made the 50% apply on top of any Section 232 duty. The 12 Chapter 38 subheadings on the list stayed on it.

changes.title: Citric acid from Canada and India: preliminary determinations
changes.detail: Commerce preliminarily found dumping by Indian exporters (98.22% all others; Daffodil Pharmachem 149.74%) but none by Jungbunzlauer Canada (0.00%). Preliminary countervailing duties of 16.50% (Canada) and 63.88% (India) have applied since June 26, 2026. Citric acid itself is Chapter 29; the order scope also reaches blends classified in 3824.99.93.
changes.now: CVD deposits; AD deposit for India (preliminary)

changes.title: Section 338: 50% on Canadian fatty acids, sorbitol and other preparations
changes.detail: Under section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, Proclamation 11048 (signed July 20, 2026) imposed +50% (9903.03.14) on listed products of Canada to offset Canada's motor-vehicle surtax on U.S. cars. Its start was suspended for three days (Proclamation 11056) and took effect at 12:01 a.m. on August 22, 2026. In Chapter 38 it covers 3811.21, 3823.11, 3823.12, 3823.13, 3823.19.20, 3823.19.40, 3823.70.40, 3823.70.60, 3824.60, 3824.99.39, 3824.99.55 and 3824.99.93, and applies even to goods entered under USMCA (U.S. note 51(a)).

changes.title: HFC blends from China: antidumping rate for Sanmei set at 182.61%
changes.detail: Final results of the 2023–2024 administrative review of the 2016 antidumping order on HFC refrigerant blends from China (R-404A, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A and R-507A): 182.61% for Zhejiang Sanmei and related companies. Other Chinese exporters pay the China-wide rate of 216.37%. The order, continued in 2022, still cites the pre-2022 numbers 3824.78.0020 and 3824.78.0050; these blends are now classified in heading 3827.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover almost all of Chapter 38
changes.detail: +10% or +12.5% on goods of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84; the EU and Taiwan a 10% floor, Japan, Korea and Switzerland a 12.5% floor). In Chapter 38 only doped wafers (3818) are on the general exemption list (note 52(b)). Goods for use in pharmaceutical applications in 32 listed subheadings are exempt if that use is shown (note 52(e)); fatty acids and fatty alcohols are exempt for the EU, Switzerland, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan and five other economies (note 52(j)); USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. Seven Chapter 38 subheadings were on its exemption list (9903.03.03): 3808.94.10 and 3808.94.50 (disinfectants, including hand sanitizer), doped wafers (3818) and 3824.91, 3824.99.29, 3824.99.49 and 3824.99.55.

changes.title: Fatty acids from Indonesia and Malaysia: preliminary countervailing duties
changes.detail: Commerce preliminarily found countervailable subsidies of 16.48% (Indonesia, all others; Musim Mas 16.47%) and 4.32% (Malaysia, all others) on certain fatty acids, after the ITC found a reasonable indication of injury in April 2026. Cash deposits apply from publication.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301 tariff: +25%
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), on top of Brazil's 12.5% under the 2026 action from July 24. In Chapter 38 only doped wafers (3818) are on its exemption list (note 50(a)(ii)); pharmaceutical-use goods of the listed subheadings are also exempt (note 50(a)(v)).

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: New statistical lines for doped silicon wafers
changes.detail: 3818.00.0095 was split into round monocrystalline silicon wafers of the semiconductor type (3818.00.0040), pseudo-square or rectangular wafers of the solar-cell type (3818.00.0045), other monocrystalline wafers (3818.00.0050) and other (3818.00.0091), with new statistical notes 2 and 3. All stay Free.

changes.title: MDI from China: antidumping order
changes.detail: Antidumping order on methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI) from China, at 87.25% for the examined Wanhua and Covestro companies and 161.61% China-wide. MDI is classified mainly in Chapters 29 and 39, but the scope says it may also enter under 3824.99.26 and 3824.99.29.

changes.title: Activated carbon from China: amended review results
changes.detail: Commerce amended the 2023–2024 review of the 2007 antidumping order on activated carbon from China (3802.10): $0.00/kg for Datong Juqiang, $0.04/kg for Ningxia Huahui and the non-examined separate-rate companies. Other Chinese exporters pay the China-wide rate of $2.42/kg. The order was continued in November 2023.

changes.title: Citric acid from China: orders continued
changes.detail: After the third sunset reviews, the 2009 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on citric acid and certain citrate salts from China were continued. The scope covers citric acid blends that enter under Chapter 38.

changes.title: No duties on active anode material (graphite) from China
changes.detail: Commerce had found dumping (93.50% for the listed exporters, 102.72% China-wide) and subsidies (66.86% all others) on active anode material — the graphite of 3801.10.50 and 3801.90.00 used in lithium-ion battery anodes — but the ITC determined that U.S. industry was not materially retarded, so no antidumping or countervailing duty orders were issued. Chinese anode material still pays the Section 301 duties (base + 37.5%).

changes.title: EPA sets 2026–2027 Renewable Fuel Standard volumes; import RIN cut deferred
changes.detail: EPA's final rule (effective June 15, 2026) set the biomass-based diesel and other RFS volumes for 2026 and 2027. It did not finalize the proposed cut of RINs for imported renewable fuel and fuel made from foreign feedstocks by half, and said it intends to adopt one from the 2028 compliance year or shortly after. It made importers of renewable fuel jointly and severally liable for RFS violations (40 CFR 80.1461(g)). EPA data in the rule show U.S. imports of biodiesel and renewable diesel fell from about 830 million gallons in 2024 to about 140 million gallons in 2025.

changes.title: Chlorinated isocyanurates from China: review results
changes.detail: Final results of the 2023–2024 review of the antidumping order on chlorinated isocyanurates (pool and spa sanitizers that can enter under 3808.94.50): 39.87% (Heze Huayi), 30.24% (Juancheng Kangtai), 285.63% China-wide. The China and Spain antidumping orders were continued in 2023 and the China countervailing duty order in November 2025.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026, except the products on its exemption list (9903.03.03), which included seven Chapter 38 subheadings.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. For Chapter 38 this removed the duties on non-USMCA goods of Canada (35%) and Mexico (25%), on goods of China, and the reciprocal tariff on goods of other countries (15% floor for the EU).

changes.title: Calcium hypochlorite from China: orders continued
changes.detail: Commerce and the ITC continued the 2015 antidumping and countervailing duty orders on calcium hypochlorite from China; tableted or blended product can enter under 3808.94.50 or 3808.99.95. The rates in the orders are 210.52% (antidumping, China-wide) and 65.85% (countervailing).

changes.title: New statistical lines for anode material and precious-metal catalysts
changes.detail: 3801.90.0000 was split to report active anode material containing silicon (3801.90.0010) separately, and 3815.12.0000 to report supported catalysts with platinum-group metals (3815.12.0010) separately. Rates did not change.

changes.title: China Section 301 product exclusions extended to November 9, 2026
changes.detail: USTR extended 178 product exclusions, including described supported catalysts of 3815.11 and 3815.19 and disinfectant wipes of 3808.94.5010, through November 9, 2026 (9903.88.69).

changes.title: Small-diameter graphite electrodes from China: order continued
changes.detail: The 2009 antidumping order on small-diameter graphite electrodes from China was continued; its scope also covers graphite pin joining systems classified in 3801.10.

changes.title: Russian aluminum: 200% Section 232 duty reaches aluminum-packed chemicals
changes.detail: From August 18, 2025, derivative aluminum articles added by Commerce's inclusions process — including 27 Chapter 38 lines such as aerosol pesticides and disinfectants, solvents, lubricant additives and antifreeze (note 19(k)) — pay 200% (9903.85.68) when they are products of Russia or contain aluminum smelted or cast in Russia. For other countries those lines are no longer on a Section 232 list in the 2026 Revision 21.

changes.title: Canada IEEPA duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 2,4-D herbicide from China and India: antidumping and countervailing duty orders
changes.detail: Orders on 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, including formulations that enter under 3808.93.05 and 3808.93.15. Antidumping cash deposits: China-wide 126.58%; India 20.62% (Atul), 3.18% (Meghmani), 11.90% (all others). Countervailing: China 26.50% (all others; Shandong Rainbow 169.63%), India 5.88% (all others).

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff covers most Chapter 38 goods
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico, from April 5, 2025. Seven Chapter 38 subheadings were on the exemption list (9903.01.32): 3808.94.10, 3808.94.50, 3818, 3824.91, 3824.99.29, 3824.99.49 and 3824.99.55. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, including Chapter 38 chemicals. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Chinese doped silicon wafers: Section 301 duty raised to 50%
changes.detail: From January 1, 2025, wafers of 3818 from China pay +50% (9903.91.05) under the four-year review, instead of the earlier list duty. USTR's December 2025 semiconductor action said the rate will rise again on June 23, 2027, by an amount to be announced.

changes.title: Biodiesel from Argentina and Indonesia: orders continued
changes.detail: After the first sunset reviews (ITC affirmative, June 8, 2023), Commerce continued the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on biodiesel from Argentina and Indonesia (3826.00.10 and 3826.00.30). CBP keeps collecting cash deposits at the rates in effect.

changes.title: Biodiesel from Argentina and Indonesia: antidumping and countervailing duty orders
changes.detail: Antidumping order (April 26, 2018) and countervailing duty order (January 4, 2018). Rates set in the orders for all other exporters: Argentina 74.63% antidumping (after subsidy offset) plus 71.87% countervailing; Indonesia 92.52% antidumping plus 38.95% countervailing.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 38 goods were **$22.15B in 2025**, -8.4% from $24.19B in 2024 and well below the 2022 peak of $29.51B. The trade is spread out: **Japan** ($3.19B, mostly 3824 preparations — $1.93B — and silicon wafers), **Canada** ($2.35B, catalysts, lubricant additives and biodiesel), **Germany** ($2.28B, down from $3.27B), **Korea** ($1.96B, mainly 3824 preparations) and **China** ($1.28B, down from $1.76B; diagnostic reagents, pesticides and graphite). Japan and Canada together supplied 25%.

By product, the 3824 preparations n.e.s. ($6.30B) and diagnostic and laboratory reagents ($5.79B, led by Germany, the UK and Singapore) make up more than half of the chapter, followed by doped wafers ($1.71B), catalysts ($1.68B) and pesticides ($1.65B).

Two shifts stand out. **Biodiesel** imports fell from $1.95B in 2024 to $106M in 2025, almost all of it from Canada ($95M): since January 1, 2025 the U.S. clean fuel production credit (section 45Z) pays only for domestically produced fuel, and the biodiesel mixture credit expired; EPA counted biodiesel and renewable diesel imports falling from about 830 million gallons in 2024 to about 140 million in 2025. **Indonesia** nearly doubled its shipments ($678M to $1.25B), mostly palm-based fatty acids and fatty alcohols ($811M in heading 3823) — the goods now under preliminary antidumping and countervailing duties.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so it predates the 2026 Section 301 and Section 338 duties. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 38: Miscellaneous Chemical Products — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Chemicals (HTS Ch. 38): EPA Pesticide & TSCA Rules, HFC Allowances, Biodiesel, AD/CVD & Ways to Lower Duty | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The entry rules for each HTS Chapter 38 line — EPA pesticide registration and Notice of Arrival, TSCA certification, HFC and ozone-depleting substance allowances, EPA fuel and RFS rules for biodiesel, FDA rules for hand sanitizer, DOT hazmat — the AD/CVD orders, and the legal ways to pay less.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Chapter 38 base rates are low (Free to 6.5%), so what decides the cost is **origin** and the extra duties: base + 37.5% for most Chinese goods (50% for wafers), 10%–12.5% from the 60 Section 301 economies, 37.5% from Brazil, and 50% on Canadian fatty acids and other listed goods. Several products also carry **antidumping or countervailing duties** that the tariff calculator does not include.

The paperwork depends on the product: pesticides and disinfectants need EPA registration and a Notice of Arrival, most other chemicals a TSCA certification, refrigerant blends EPA allowances, biodiesel EPA fuel and Renewable Fuel Standard compliance, hand sanitizer FDA drug rules, and flammable or compressed products DOT hazmat handling. Each rule and lever below links to its regulation.

levers.title: Know the country of origin — it moves the total more than the base rate
levers.saves: Up to 37.5 points: the same 5% herbicide pays 42.5% from China or Brazil, 15%–17.5% from most Section 301 economies, 10% from the EU, and 5% from a country outside the 60 economies
levers.document: Commercial invoice and production records showing where the product was made. For mixtures and formulations, origin follows where the goods were last substantially transformed; ask CBP for a binding ruling when Chinese active ingredients are formulated elsewhere.
levers.caveat: Simple dilution or repacking does not change origin. AD/CVD orders follow their own scope and country rules, separate from the tariff origin.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20 and 52

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican goods
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on Canada or Mexico plus the base rate (up to 6.5%); not the 50% Section 338 duty on the 12 listed Canadian subheadings
levers.appliesTo: All lines, for originating goods of Canada or Mexico
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer; it need not follow a prescribed format and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: The Section 338 duty on Canadian fatty acids, fatty alcohols, sorbitol and the other listed goods applies even with a USMCA claim. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51 and 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Enter pharmaceutical-use chemicals under the Section 301 exemption
levers.saves: The 10% or 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (and Brazil's 25%) on goods for use in pharmaceutical applications
levers.document: Entry under 9903.05.89 (or 9903.05.06 for Brazil) with records showing the goods are for use in pharmaceutical applications.
levers.caveat: The exemption depends on the end use, not the product; it does not lift China's 2018–2019 list duties. Keep evidence of use in case CBP asks.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 52(e) and 50(a)(v)

levers.title: Source fatty acids and fatty alcohols from an exempted economy
levers.saves: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duty on stearic acid, oleic acid, palm/coconut fatty acids and 3823.70.40 fatty alcohols
levers.appliesTo: 3823.11, 3823.12, 3823.19.20, 3823.70.40 from the EU, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, Cambodia, Ecuador, Jordan (and some lines from Switzerland, Guatemala and El Salvador)
levers.document: Proof of origin in one of the listed economies; enter under that economy's exception heading (e.g. 9903.05.97 EU, 9903.05.99 Malaysia, 9903.06.16 Indonesia).
levers.caveat: Tall oil fatty acids (3823.13), 3823.19.40 and oleyl alcohol are not on these lists. From Canada the same lines pay 50% under Section 338.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(j)

levers.title: Use a China Section 301 product exclusion while it lasts
levers.saves: The 25% List 3 duty on the excluded products, until November 9, 2026
levers.appliesTo: Described supported catalysts of 3815.11 and 3815.19; disinfectant wipes of 3808.94.5010 (China)
levers.document: Entry under 9903.88.69 for a product matching the exclusion's description in U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii).
levers.caveat: The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty still applies. The exclusions expire at 11:59 p.m. on November 9, 2026 unless USTR extends them.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20(vvv)

levers.title: Claim an FTA rate for the base duty
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 6.5%) for originating goods of Korea, Australia, Singapore, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Panama, Israel, Jordan, Morocco, Oman or Bahrain
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines whose Special column lists the partner
levers.document: The origin documentation the agreement requires (19 CFR parts 10 and 102 and the agreement's rules of origin in the HTSUS general notes).
levers.caveat: An FTA claim does not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty: Korea pays a 12.5% floor, Australia, Chile and others +12.5% on top. GSP (A, A*, A+) is not available — Congress has not renewed it.

citations.label: HTSUS General Notes (FTA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim drawback when imported chemicals are exported or used in exported goods
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on goods that are re-exported, unused or used to make exported products (19 CFR 191.3 lists the duties that qualify)
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191).
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)).

levers.title: Check the AD/CVD scope before you buy
levers.saves: The whole antidumping or countervailing duty, when the product is outside the order
levers.appliesTo: Biodiesel (Argentina, Indonesia), activated carbon, HFC blends, 2,4-D, pool chlorine and graphite electrodes (China and others), fatty acids (Indonesia, Malaysia, preliminary) and the 3824.99 preparations named in the orders
levers.document: The order's written scope (it, not the HTS number, decides). When unsure, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: A product inside the scope pays the cash deposit even if entered under a different HTS line; Commerce can also find circumvention through third countries.

rules.title: Pesticides and disinfectants: file EPA's Notice of Arrival of Pesticides and Devices before the shipment arrives; EPA tells CBP to release or refuse it
Pesticide products must be registered under FIFRA before they are sold or distributed, and imported pesticides must be registered to be admitted
Chemical substances and mixtures: TSCA import certification (positive or negative) filed before release
HFC refrigerant blends: bulk imports need EPA consumption or application-specific allowances, and shipment data filed 10 days (vessel) or 5 days (other) before importation
Blends with CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, methyl bromide or HCFCs: imports limited to EPA allowances and exemptions
Biodiesel and biodiesel blends imported as diesel fuel: importer must meet the diesel fuel standards (15 ppm sulfur)
Renewable Fuel Standard: RINs for imported biodiesel are generated by the importer or a registered foreign producer; importers are jointly liable for RFS violations
Biodiesel suitable for use as diesel fuel: federal fuel excise tax is due on entry unless entered by bulk transfer by a registrant (not in the tariff calculator)
Hand sanitizer (3808.94.50.80) is a drug: it must meet FDA requirements, and the foreign establishment that makes it must be registered with FDA
Flammable solvents and thinners, many pesticides and alcohol sanitizers, and refrigerant gases in cylinders: hazardous materials for shipping papers, marking and packaging
Biodiesel from Argentina and Indonesia: antidumping and countervailing duty cash deposits (orders since 2018, continued 2023; not in the tariff calculator)
Activated carbon from China: antidumping duty per kilogram ($2.42/kg China-wide; not in the tariff calculator)
HFC blends R-404A, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A and R-507A from China: antidumping duty (216.37% China-wide; not in the tariff calculator)
2,4-D formulations (China, India), chlorinated isocyanurates (China, Spain) and calcium hypochlorite (China): antidumping and countervailing duties (not in the tariff calculator)
Fatty acids from Indonesia and Malaysia: preliminary antidumping and countervailing duty cash deposits since July–September 2026 (not in the tariff calculator)
Graphite electrodes from China (order) and large-diameter electrodes from China and India (preliminary): AD/CVD can reach 3801 goods; no order on active anode material (not in the tariff calculator)
Orders whose scope reaches 3824.99 blends and preparations — citric acid (China; preliminary for Canada and India) and MDI (China), among others: check the scope (not in the tariff calculator)
CBS rubber accelerator from China (preliminary CVD, 3812.10): cash deposits (not in the tariff calculator)

groups.label: Artificial graphite & carbon pastes
groups.note: Graphite from China pays 37.5% on top of the base rate. Graphite electrode orders (small-diameter, China) and the 2026 large-diameter investigation (China, India) list 3801 numbers; the ITC rejected duties on Chinese active anode material in April 2026.

groups.label: Activated carbon
groups.note: Activated carbon from China is under an antidumping order since 2007 ($2.42/kg China-wide).

groups.label: Pesticides, herbicides & disinfectants
groups.note: Pesticides and disinfectants are regulated under FIFRA, so they file EPA's Notice of Arrival instead of a TSCA certification; hand sanitizer is an FDA-regulated drug. 2,4-D (China, India), chlorinated isocyanurates (China, Spain) and calcium hypochlorite (China) carry AD/CVD orders whose scopes reach 3808 formulations.

groups.label: Rubber accelerators, plasticizers & stabilizers
groups.note: CBS rubber accelerator from China is under a preliminary countervailing duty (October 2026).

groups.label: Doped silicon wafers & electronic chemicals
groups.note: Wafers are on every 2026 exemption list; only China (50%) and Russia (35% + Column 2 rules) pay extra.

groups.label: Industrial fatty acids & fatty alcohols
groups.note: From Canada most of these lines pay the 50% Section 338 duty, even under USMCA; from the EU, Malaysia and Indonesia several are exempt from Section 301. Fatty acids from Indonesia and Malaysia have paid preliminary AD/CVD cash deposits since July–September 2026.

groups.label: Other chemical preparations (n.e.s.)
groups.note: Several orders (citric acid, MDI and others) say the subject product may enter under 3824.99; the order's scope, not the HTS number, decides.

groups.label: Biodiesel
groups.note: Imported biodiesel does not earn the U.S. clean fuel production credit (section 45Z), which covers only domestically produced fuel; the biodiesel mixture credit expired after 2024. Biodiesel from Argentina and Indonesia is under antidumping and countervailing duty orders (2018, continued 2023).

groups.label: Refrigerant & other halogenated blends
groups.note: Blends containing HFCs fall under the AIM Act allowance system (40 CFR part 84); blends with CFCs, halons or HCFCs under the ozone rules (40 CFR part 82). HFC blends R-404A, R-407A, R-407C, R-410A and R-507A from China are under a 2016 antidumping order.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. AD/CVD rates are company-specific and change with each administrative review; check Commerce's latest notice and CBP's cash-deposit instructions before importing.

seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about chemical tariffs: tariffs on chemicals from China and India, the Canada Section 338 list, what happened to the Trump tariffs on chemicals, biodiesel duties, and HS codes for pesticides, hand sanitizer, activated carbon, refrigerant blends, silicon wafers and fatty acids.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on Chapter 38 chemical imports — by country, by product and by HS code. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Chapter 38 base rates are Free to 6.5%, but since July 24, 2026 the 2026 Section 301 tariffs add 10%–12.5% on goods of 60 economies (12.5% total for Japan and Korea, 10% for the EU); only doped wafers are exempt for everyone.

Chinese chemicals pay base + 37.5% on most lines (wafers 50%), and listed Canadian goods — fatty acids, fatty alcohols, sorbitol and some others — pay 50% under Section 338 even with USMCA. The 2025 IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026.

Antidumping and countervailing duties apply on top for biodiesel (Argentina, Indonesia), activated carbon, HFC blends, pool chlorine and 2,4-D (China and others), with preliminary deposits on Indonesian and Malaysian fatty acids. The tariff calculator does not include them.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on chemicals from China?
faqs.answer: For Chapter 38, most Chinese goods pay the base rate plus 25% (Section 301 List 3) plus 12.5% (the 2026 Section 301 action) — 42.5% for a 5% herbicide. Fatty acids, fatty alcohols and sorbitol pay base + 7.5% + 12.5% (List 4A), culture media and diagnostic reagents base + 12.5%, and doped silicon wafers 50%. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026. Activated carbon, HFC blends, pool chlorine, 2,4-D and several 3824 preparations also carry antidumping or countervailing duties.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on chemicals from India?
searchedAs: us tariff on chemicals from india
faqs.answer: The base rate plus 10% (9903.05.44) under the 2026 Section 301 action, in force since July 24, 2026 — for example 15% on a 5% herbicide. Doped wafers and chemicals for pharmaceutical use in the listed subheadings are exempt. Some Indian products also face antidumping or countervailing duties: 2,4-D (orders since May 2025) and, preliminarily, citric acid and large-diameter graphite electrodes.

faqs.question: What is the Section 338 tariff on Canada, and which chemicals are on the list?
faqs.answer: Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 lets the President offset a country's discrimination against U.S. commerce. Proclamation 11048 imposed +50% (9903.03.14) on the goods of Canada listed in U.S. note 51(b)(3) to Chapter 99, effective August 22, 2026. In Chapter 38 the list covers 3811.21 (lubricating-oil additives with petroleum oils), 3823.11, 3823.12, 3823.13, 3823.19.20, 3823.19.40, 3823.70.40 and 3823.70.60 (fatty acids and fatty alcohols), 3824.60 (sorbitol) and 3824.99.39, 3824.99.55 and 3824.99.93. The 50% applies even to goods entered under USMCA.

faqs.question: What happened to the Trump tariffs on chemicals?
faqs.answer: The 2025 IEEPA tariffs — 25% (later 35%) on non-USMCA Canadian goods, 25% on non-USMCA Mexican goods, the China duties and the reciprocal tariff (a 15% floor for the EU) — ended on February 24, 2026 after the Supreme Court ruled IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. A 10% Section 122 surcharge followed until July 23, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 the Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies apply (10%–12.5%), China's 2018–2019 Section 301 duties continue, and since August 22, 2026 some Canadian chemicals pay 50% under Section 338.

faqs.question: What is HTS Chapter 38?
faqs.answer: Chapter 38 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, "Miscellaneous chemical products", has 27 headings (3801–3827) and 217 ten-digit U.S. lines: graphite, activated carbon, tall oil, rosin, pesticides and disinfectants, finishing agents, fluxes, additives, rubber chemicals, catalysts, doped wafers, brake fluid, antifreeze, culture media, diagnostic reagents, fatty acids and alcohols, chemical preparations n.e.s., waste, biodiesel and halogenated refrigerant blends. Base rates run from Free to 6.5%.

faqs.question: What does HS code 3824.99 cover?
faqs.answer: 3824.99 is the residual subheading for chemical products and preparations of the chemical or allied industries not specified elsewhere — cultured crystals, mixtures of inorganic compounds (including lithium nickel cobalt manganese oxides), fatty-substance mixtures, petroleum-based mixtures, halogenated hydrocarbon mixtures, naphthenic acids and many others, split into 3824.99.11 to 3824.99.93. Rates run from Free to 6.5%. It was the largest Chapter 38 product in 2025 at $6.05B of imports, mostly from Japan and Korea.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for pesticides, herbicides and disinfectants?
faqs.answer: Heading 3808 when put up for retail sale or as preparations: insecticides 3808.91, fungicides 3808.92, herbicides 3808.93 (glyphosate mixtures 3808.93.50.20), disinfectants 3808.94 and rodenticides and others 3808.99; products with substances listed in subheading notes 1 and 2 go to 3808.52–3808.69. Rates are Free to 6.5%. Imports need EPA registration and a Notice of Arrival filed before the shipment arrives (19 CFR 12.112).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for hand sanitizer?
searchedAs: hs code for hand sanitizer gel
hs code for alcohol hand sanitizer
faqs.answer: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer with 60% or more ethanol by weight is 3808.94.50.80 (disinfectants), base rate 5%; statistical note 1 says it must meet FDA requirements. Disinfectant wipes other than paper or nonwoven wipes are 3808.94.50.10. From China hand sanitizer pays 42.5%; from Section 301 economies base + 10% or 12.5%, unless shown to be for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)).

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for activated carbon?
searchedAs: hs code for coconut shell activated carbon
faqs.answer: 3802.10.00 — 4.8% base, split into coal-based (.10), coconut-based (.20) and other (.50). Chinese activated carbon pays 4.8% + 37.5% = 42.3% plus an antidumping duty under the 2007 order ($2.42/kg China-wide); Indian and Sri Lankan activated carbon pays base + 10%. U.S. imports were $276M in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and U.S. tariff for biodiesel?
faqs.answer: 3826.00.10 for pure biodiesel (B100, 4.6%) and 3826.00.30 for blends with less than 70% petroleum oil (6.5%). Argentina and Indonesia pay base + 10% plus antidumping and countervailing duties under 2018 orders continued in 2023. Imports fell from $1.95B in 2024 to $106M in 2025 after the U.S. clean fuel production credit (45Z) was limited to domestic fuel.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for refrigerant blends like R-410A?
searchedAs: hs code for refrigerant gas r410a
hs code for refrigerant gas r404a
hs code for refrigerant gas r407c
faqs.answer: Blends go to heading 3827 by mass composition (3.7% base): 15% or more HFC-143a, as in R-404A and R-507A, is 3827.61; 40% or more HFC-125, as in R-410A (50% HFC-32, 50% HFC-125), is 3827.63; 30% or more HFC-134a, as in R-407C, is 3827.64. Single gases such as R-32 or R-134a are in Chapter 29. Bulk HFC imports need EPA allowances, and these blends from China are under an antidumping order (216.37% China-wide).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on silicon wafers?
faqs.answer: Doped silicon wafers are 3818.00.00 (round semiconductor-type 3818.00.00.40, pseudo-square solar-type .45), base rate Free. They are on the exemption lists of the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil actions, so wafers from Japan, Taiwan, Korea or Germany pay nothing. Chinese wafers pay 50% (9903.91.05), which USTR said will rise on June 23, 2027; Russian wafers pay 35%. U.S. imports were $1.71B in 2025, $707M from Japan.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on graphite from China?
faqs.answer: Artificial graphite and anode material (3801.10, 3801.90) from China pay the base rate (Free to 4.9%) plus 25% (List 3) plus 12.5%. In April 2026 the ITC rejected antidumping and countervailing duties on Chinese active anode material, so no order applies; graphite electrode orders and a 2026 investigation of large-diameter electrodes can reach 3801 goods. Natural graphite is heading 2504 (Chapter 25).

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for stearic acid and other fatty acids?
searchedAs: hs code for palm fatty acid distillate
faqs.answer: Heading 3823: stearic acid 3823.11 (2.1¢/kg + 3.8%), oleic acid 3823.12, tall oil fatty acids 3823.13, palm, palm-kernel or coconut fatty acids and acid oils 3823.19.20 (2.3%), industrial fatty alcohols 3823.70. Most pay base + 10% under Section 301, but the EU, Malaysia, Indonesia and some others are exempt on several lines; from Canada they pay 50% (Section 338). Indonesian and Malaysian fatty acids also carry preliminary AD/CVD deposits.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import Chapter 38 chemicals from?
faqs.answer: From many places: Japan ($3.19B), Canada ($2.35B), Germany ($2.28B), Korea ($1.96B), China ($1.28B) and Indonesia ($1.25B) led the $22.15B imported in 2025, followed by the UK, Mexico, France and Singapore.
